newsitem.title: GERMANY: Mark rise hurts German trade long-term - Bundesbank.
newsitem.headline: Mark rise hurts German trade long-term - Bundesbank.

text.p: A rise in the external value of the mark ultimately has the effect of worsening Germany's trade balance, but the short-term impact of mark gains can often be overshadowed by other factors, the Bundesbank said.

The German central bank said in its monthly report for January that the impact of mark gains was often delayed, as factors such as the need to maintain market share meant companies often delayed passing on increases in costs to customers.

Working on the assumption that a rise in the domestic currency -- which makes exports dearer and imports cheaper -- should normally lead to a smaller trade surplus or increased deficit, the Bundesbank analysed exchange rate and trade patterns over the last 20 years.

"The overall result shows that the German external trade balance reacts normally to exchange rate changes, that means that a real appreciation (in the currency) is countered in the long term by a worsening of the external trade balance and vice versa," the Bundesbank said.
But it added that other factors, such as overall economic growth and the development of world trade, played a key role.

"In a comparison of the derived reaction pattern with the actual developments in the German trade balance over the last 20 years...one must however note that in addition to the exchange rate effects which are the primary focus of the study, there are other important influential factors," it said.
This meant that a link between the exchange rate and trade was not easy to spot "with the naked eye", it added.

In 1995, the German trade account surplus had shown an increase of 19 billion marks despite the sharp rise in the mark, which hit an all-time high against the dollar in March of that year. Export trade was only hit notably from autumn on.

The Bundesbank said this collapse in exports late in the year -- which was worse than might have been expected on the basis of the mark's rise alone -- was clearly linked to a weakening of growth in Germany and its trade partner countries.
The behaviour of companies themselves often contributed to delays in the response of trade to exchange rate swings. Little price reaction was seen when the fluctuation was only brief.
But companies also sometimes hesitated to raise prices for some time for fear of losing market share, the Bundesbank said. Futures and other hedging tools helped make this bearable.

"Such strategies must always appear advantageous if the costs of winning back market share later are estimated as being higher than the loss of profit sustained as a result, which may only be temporary," the Bundesbank said.
Yet price increases were almost inevitable in the longer term if the exchange rates conditions persisted, it said.

"In the longer term, the price adjustment is supported by the fact that lasting losses from export trade cannot be borne," it said. "In the long term no company can afford to produce at costs which cannot be covered in its sales markets."

Despite the high degree of integration in European markets, companies were more likely to pass on exchange rate costs quickly within the European Union than in trade with countries outside this area, the Bundesbank said.
Its study showed that only 31 percent of increased costs were passed on to non-EU buyers, but 45 percent in the EU.
"The reason for this could lie in the considerable swings in the mark's value against the major world currencies whereas the volatility against EU currencies is much smaller," it said.

Companies may also be less adequately hedged within the EU area due to the "illusion" that European currency rates were already fixed against each other, it said. This would make it more difficult for them to absorb unfavourable exchange rates.
